title: Towards Reliable VLM Judges: State-Conditional Invariance and Presentation-Aware Diagnostics
claim: A diagnostic benchmark pipeline shows that stability under presentation changes alone does not guarantee a judge responds to causal changes.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right flow, simulators to variants to judges to verdicts, dashed callout
description: A wide, single-panel diagram that reads left to right. At the far left, a blue box lists three simulators (MiniGrid, MiniWorld, Habitat) with a Metadata box beneath it. Arrows lead to three rows labeled Full, Re-present and Counterfactual. Each row shows four small grid-world frames (start, key, door, final). The Re-present row also shows distorted versions, labeled format, order, style, wording and cue mask. Orange headers C1–C4 run along the top, naming the four diagnostic conditions. The frames feed into a VLM-as-a-Judge column of model logos. These produce verdict and key pairs. Two rows show S/S in green, and the third shows S/F in red. A cyan check marks consistency and a red cross marks failed causal discrimination. A Metrics bar sits at top right. A sample question box sits at the bottom. A dashed box at lower right reads Consistency ≠ Reliability.
caption: Overview of GridWM-Judge. The framework integrates simulator-based exam generation, VLM judging, and automatic scoring to assess four SCI diagnostic conditions (C1--C4). Ground-truth metadata are hidden from judges and used for scoring. The example illustrates that presentation consistency alone does not guarantee causal discrimination or reliable judging.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.
